Title: Estimating Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio by instrumented indentation test - ScienceDirect
The estimate of Young's modulus from instrumented indentation test results relies on knowing in advance the Poisson's ratio of the sample's material. In this paper we show how an empirical correlation between hardness and elastic moduli, along with the usual instrumented indentation test, allows the estimation of both Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio (and, from them, the bulk and shear moduli) for homogeneous and isotropic samples. The results obtained in this work indicate that the proposed approach represents an improvement over previous practices for the estimation of *E* and *ν* from indentation tests, particularly for hard ceramic materials in case no previous information on Poisson's ratio is available. results.title: Hardness, Stiffness & Strength: Exploring Mechanical Properties of Materials | AT-Machining
results.content: # Hardness, Stiffness & Strength: Exploring Mechanical Properties of Materials. Material properties are pivotal characteristics of every material that determine how they performs under external forces (changes in shape and form). In CNC machining, hardness, stiffness, and strength are three essential material properties that define how a material reacts when it comes in contact with the CNC cutting tools. This guide delves into the fundamentals of hardness, stiffness, and strength, exploring their relevance to material selection in product development. Material hardness refers to the resistance of a material’s surface to localized surface deformation or its ability to resist a pointed tool’s penetration. This property is critical when determining a suitable metal in applications with two metals impacting each other- the one with high rigidity will cause plastic deformation or scratch the less hard one. Diamond is a typical material with high hardness and is commonly used for **CNC machining tools**.

results.title: Analysis of Indentation by an Indenter - Sanfoundry
results.content:
Title: Analysis of Indentation by an Indenter - Sanfoundry
In this guide, you will learn about indentation testing, including the effects of different indenter shapes, stress comparisons between hardness and compression tests, and load prediction for solids. You’ll also compare Prandtl’s and Shaw-DeSalvo’s deformation models and explore how Hertz theory applies to indentation mechanics. Indentation tests apply a known force through a hard, standardized indenter, usually made of diamond or hardened steel, to a material’s surface. The shape and material of the indenter influence the stress distribution during the test. * **Conical Indenter:** Used in Vickers and Rockwell tests, it generates a sharp point, focusing the applied force over a smaller area, leading to higher localized stresses and deeper penetration for harder materials. Beneath the indentation in a hardness test, there is a plastic zone. * The upward flow of the material compensates for the material displaced by the indentation made in hardness test. * A more accurate deformation model was developed by **Shaw and DeSalvo** to better describe material behavior under a Brinell indenter. * The model predicts the formation of a plastic zone directly beneath the indenter. In hardness testing, Hertz theory can be used to derive the stress distribution beneath a spherical indenter, such as in the Brinell test. This analysis provides a more accurate representation of the material’s resistance to indentation and explains the behavior observed in real-world hardness tests. * Indentation testing applies a known force through an indenter, and the size or depth of the indentation is measured to determine hardness, using techniques like Brinell, Rockwell, and Vickers for different materials. * In hardness tests, the plastic zone is constrained by the surrounding elastic material, requiring higher compressive stress than in compression tests due to elastic hindrance. * The Shaw and DeSalvo model describes deformation under a Brinell indenter more accurately by focusing on a plastic zone beneath the indenter, with minimal material flow around the indentation, unlike Prandtl’s model. * Hertz theory in contact mechanics relates contact stress to applied force, Young’s modulus, and radii of curvature, predicting stress distribution beneath spherical indenters like those used in Brinell tests.

results.title: Indentation - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: In subject area:Materials Science. Indentation is defined as a technique used to probe the mechanical properties of solid state materials by measuring their surface response to the penetration of a probe with known geometry and imposed load. It allows for the investigation of hardness and elastic stiffness, as well as size and strain rate effects. Indentation is a very versatile, easy to implement and powerful tool to probe the mechanical properties of the surface of the ceramic materials, with local resolution. Indentation is one of the main techniques for probing mechanical properties of engineering materials. Compared with the tension/compression tests, an indentation test is ultra-local and less invasive, in which the indenter is pushed into the surface of the sample. As all mechanical and nanotribological properties of materials are temperature-dependent, primarily owing to the increased phonon activities, thermal fluctuation, and phase transformation, small-scale characterization of materials using nanoindentation/scratching at finite temperatures would open up substantial new possibilities in nanomechanics to understand material behaviour at service temperatures and conditions relevant to industrial applications [2,3].
